Norwegian-CDI-WG-production

KM

2024-10-10

As a preparation we first load required libraries and functions:

Data preparation

There are three key objects needed for all the analyses done and presented here:

  1. responses matrix (self explanatory)
  2. cdi data frame (item information)
  3. scores data frame (participant information: raw scores $ demographics)

We import responses, items, and participant data from local files, which in turn are downloaded from WordBank, exclude non norming (longitudinal?) data, and perform a check (our sums equal to imported scores).

# We get responses and item data:
# wordbankr::get_instrument_data("Norwegian", "WG", item_info=T, administration_info = T) %>% filter(is_norming) -> norwegian_wb_wg
# write_csv(norwegian_wb_wg, file = file.path("Data", "norwegian_wb_wg.csv"))

# More item data available, if needed: modify select():
read_csv("Data/norwegian_wb_wg.csv") %>%
  dplyr::filter(item_kind == "word") %>%
  select(child_id, item_id, item_definition, english_gloss, value) -> responses
## Rows: 1104162 Columns: 23
## ── Column specification ────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
## Delimiter: ","
## chr  (13): item_id, value, language, form, form_type, item_kind, category, i...
## dbl   (3): data_id, age, child_id
## lgl   (6): produces, understands, complexity_category, comprehension, produc...
## date  (1): date_of_test
## 
## ℹ Use `spec()` to retrieve the full column specification for this data.
## ℹ Specify the column types or set `show_col_types = FALSE` to quiet this message.
# We get items (Norwegian, English glosses, and IDs):
responses %>% distinct(item_definition, english_gloss, item_id) -> cdi

# We recode responses into zeroes and ones:
if_else(is.na(responses$value) | responses$value == "understands", 0, 1) -> responses$value

# We get scores and demo data.
# wordbankr::get_administration_data("Norwegian", form = "WG",
#   include_demographic_info = T,
#   include_birth_info = T,
#   include_health_conditions = T,
#   include_language_exposure = T,
#   include_study_internal_id = T) -> norwegian_wb_participants
# write_csv(norwegian_wb_participants, file = file.path("Data", "norwegian_wb_participants.csv"))

# More demo data available, if needed: modify select():
read_csv("Data/norwegian_wb_participants.csv") %>%
  filter(form == "WG" & is_norming) %>%
  select(child_id, age, sex, production) -> scores
## Rows: 12029 Columns: 22
## ── Column specification ────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
## Delimiter: ","
## chr   (6): language, form, dataset_name, birth_order, caregiver_education, sex
## dbl   (4): child_id, age, comprehension, production
## lgl  (11): is_norming, ethnicity, race, birth_weight, born_early_or_late, ge...
## date  (1): downloaded
## 
## ℹ Use `spec()` to retrieve the full column specification for this data.
## ℹ Specify the column types or set `show_col_types = FALSE` to quiet this message.
# We recode sex (just because we used girl/boy before):
if_else(scores$sex == "Female", "girl",
        if_else(scores$sex == "Male", "boy", scores$sex)) -> scores$sex

# We don't need to filter out longitudinal data, as we used is_norming condition.
# Otherwise some filtering might be needed here.

# We check the sums (should return zero tibble):
responses %>% group_by(child_id) %>% summarise(score = sum(value)) %>%
  full_join(scores) %>% filter(score != production)
## Joining with `by = join_by(child_id)`
## # A tibble: 0 × 5
## # ℹ 5 variables: child_id <dbl>, score <dbl>, age <dbl>, sex <chr>,
## #   production <dbl>

We prepare the responses matrix (eliminating all 0’s and all 1’s items).

Mirt documentation suggests however removing items with difficulties > .95 and < .05. Check and explore in the future.

responses %>% group_by(item_id) %>% filter(var(value) > 0) %>%
  pivot_wider(names_from = "item_id", values_from = "value", id_cols = "child_id") -> responses

# We recalculate scores here to maintain the response matrix row order
# (which seems to be messed up with in the process of pivoting above):
responses %>% rowwise() %>% mutate(score = sum(across(starts_with("item_")))) %>%
     select(1, last_col()) %>% left_join(scores) %>% select(- last_col()) -> scores
## Joining with `by = join_by(child_id)`
responses <- as.matrix(select(responses, starts_with("item_")))
cdi %>% filter(item_id %in% colnames(responses)) -> cdi

print(paste0("There are ", nrow(responses), " parents, ", ncol(responses),
             " items (out of ", nrow(cdi), ") with non-zero variance, and ",
             length(which(is.na(responses))), " missing responses."))
## [1] "There are 2258 parents, 395 items (out of 395) with non-zero variance, and 0 missing responses."

Model creation

For the model creation we start by deciding on the optimal number of quadrature points. With a set number of quadrature points we proceed to fitting the model iteratively, first removing any items without a fit, and then removing all items showing high local dependence and fitting the model again. We continue with removing misfits and locally dependent items if needed.

Quadrature points

We decide on the number of quadrature points iteratively by fitting models with increasing numbers and comparing their fit. We start with the default and increase it in a number of arbitrary, but hopefully not unreasonable, steps.

We also compare the parameter estimates for the first item, just out of curosity: as the goodness of fit stabilises, so should the estimates.

It may take some time! Switch eval on only if you really need to recalculate.

quadpts <- quadpts_comp(responses, quadpts = c(61, 151, 301, 451, 601, 751), NCYCLES = 100000,
             output_file = "Data/norwegian_wg_prod_quadpts.RData")

We load the comparison of model fits for different numbers of quadrature points from a file. Here there are:

load("Data/norwegian_wg_prod_quadpts.RData")
quadpts[1:3,]
##         [,1]      [,2]      [,3]      [,4]      [,5]      [,6]     
## quadpts 61        151       301       451       601       751      
## conv    TRUE      TRUE      TRUE      TRUE      TRUE      TRUE     
## logLik  -109991.2 -109828.7 -109826.7 -109826.7 -109826.7 -109826.7

And here are the parameter estimates for the first item:

sapply(1:ncol(quadpts), function(x) quadpts[,x]$item1pars)
##         [,1]      [,2]      [,3]      [,4]      [,5]      [,6]
## a1  2.171376  2.538064  2.621524  2.621397  2.621457  2.621841
## d  -1.225836 -1.162001 -1.087991 -1.088116 -1.088696 -1.088150
quadtp <- 301

Based on the above we set the number of quadrature points to 301.

Model fitting, round 1

We iteratively fit the model and remove any misfits until we have fits for all items.

It may take some time!

We save the model to a file to save time in the future (if you want to refit the model, switch the eval on):

model <- misfits_removal(responses=responses, quadtps=quadtp, NCYCLES=100000, p=0.001,
                          output_file = "Data/norwegian_wg_prod.RData")

We load the model from a file and print a basic summary:

load("Data/norwegian_wg_prod.RData")
mod <- model[[1]]
items_removed <- model[[2]]
rm(model) # to save space

mod
## 
## Call:
## mirt(data = responses, model = 1, SE = TRUE, quadpts = quadtps, 
##     technical = list(NCYCLES = NCYCLES))
## 
## Full-information item factor analysis with 1 factor(s).
## Converged within 1e-04 tolerance after 1914 EM iterations.
## mirt version: 1.42 
## M-step optimizer: BFGS 
## EM acceleration: Ramsay 
## Number of rectangular quadrature: 301
## Latent density type: Gaussian 
## 
## Information matrix estimated with method: Oakes
## Second-order test: model is a possible local maximum
## Condition number of information matrix =  4164.658
## 
## Log-likelihood = -109137.5
## Estimated parameters: 784 
## AIC = 219842.9
## BIC = 224329.2; SABIC = 221838.3
## G2 (9999999216) = 187610.7, p = 1
## RMSEA = 0, CFI = NaN, TLI = NaN

Items fit

3 items were misfits in the process of model fitting and were removed in 2 iterations before a model with no misfits was obtained.

cdi %>% filter(item_id %in% unlist(items_removed))
## # A tibble: 3 × 3
##   item_definition english_gloss     item_id 
##   <chr>           <chr>             <chr>   
## 1 morfar          grandfather       item_262
## 2 oldemor         great grandmother item_265
## 3 blå             blue              item_341
if(length(items_removed)) {
  responses <- responses[, -which((colnames(responses) %in% unlist(items_removed)))]
  cdi %>% filter(! item_id %in% unlist(items_removed)) -> cdi
  if (nrow(cdi) == ncol(responses)) print(paste0(ncol(responses), " items left after removal."))
}
## [1] "392 items left after removal."

Local dependence

Check and explore the following code in the future (also compare with Kachergis et al., 2022)

# I can't make the following code hide the results...
residuals <- residuals(mod, df.p=FALSE) # TODO: explore other parameters?
save(residuals, file = "Data/norwegian_wg_prod_residuals.RData")
load("Data/norwegian_wg_prod_residuals.RData")
residuals_up <- residuals
residuals_up[lower.tri(residuals_up)] <- NA # upper diagonal contains signed Cramers V coefficients
hist(residuals_up, main="Histogram of signed Cramer's V coefficients", xlab= "Cramer's V")

summary(as.vector(residuals_up))[-7]
##        Min.     1st Qu.      Median        Mean     3rd Qu.        Max. 
## -0.17990485 -0.07691781 -0.06857981 -0.04648808 -0.05273426  0.53771920
# -7 to avoid reporting NAs, which would be confusing as lower triangle is filled with them

To display the most highly mutually dependent items we use V > .3 as the threshold:

indexes <- arrayInd(which(residuals_up > 0.3), dim(residuals))
data.frame(item1 = pull(cdi[indexes[, 1], "english_gloss"]),
           item2 = pull(cdi[indexes[, 2], "english_gloss"]), CramersV = residuals_up[indexes])
##   item1 item2  CramersV
## 1 mommy daddy 0.5377192

There are a few but following Kachergis et al. we set the threshold for removing items to V > .5 and we remove the following items:

indexes <- arrayInd(which(residuals_up > 0.5), dim(residuals))
data.frame(item1 = pull(cdi[indexes[, 1], "item_definition"]),
           item2 = pull(cdi[indexes[, 2], "item_definition"]), CramersV = residuals_up[indexes])
##   item1 item2  CramersV
## 1 mamma pappa 0.5377192
unique(as.vector(indexes)) -> items_to_remove_ids
if(length(items_to_remove_ids)) {
     responses[, -items_to_remove_ids] -> responses
     cdi[-items_to_remove_ids,] -> cdi
}

Model fitting, round 2

Then we repeat the iterative model fit with misfits removal.

model <- misfits_removal(responses=responses, quadtps=quadtp, NCYCLES=100000, p=0.001,
                          output_file = "Data/norwegian_wg_prod_2.RData")
beep()

We load the model from a file (comment out if just fitted above) and print a basic summary:

load("Data/norwegian_wg_prod_2.RData")
mod <- model[[1]]
items_removed <- model[[2]]
rm(model) # to save space

mod

Items fit

Model exploration

IRT items parameters

params_IRT <- as.data.frame(coef(mod, simplify = TRUE, IRTpars = TRUE)$items)[1:2]
cdi <- cbind(params_IRT, cdi)

Scatterplot of difficulty by discrimination (we use English glosses; also, if we had categories we could add them as colours):

Ability vs. raw scores

We estimate ability levels for children from the sample based on the model.

scores <- cbind(scores, fscores(mod, method = "MAP", full.scores.SE = TRUE))
## Warning: The following factor score estimates failed to converge successfully:
##     2126

Explore the failed convergence? Does it have something to do with the chosen MAP method?

Plot the estimated ability level against raw scores:

ggplot(scores, aes(score, F1)) +
  geom_point() +
  ylab("Ability level (theta)") +
  xlab("Raw score (sum of checked items)") +
  ylim(-4, 4) +
  theme(
  panel.background = element_rect(fill = NA),
  panel.grid.major = element_line(colour = "lightgrey"),
  text = element_text(size=16)
)

The scatterplot above shows that IRT estimates get “normalised”, compared to raw scores, as can be seen on the following histograms (flat distribution for raw scores vs. bell-like distribution for theta estimates).

# Should be in two separate chunks perhaps?
hist(scores$score, xlab = "Raw sums", main = "")
hist(scores$F1, xlab = "Estimated ability levels", main = "")

Ability vs. SE

Plot the ability level against SE:

ggplot(scores, aes(F1, SE_F1)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.3) +
  xlab("Ability level (theta)") +
  ylab("Standard error (SE)") +
  labs(title = "Norwegian CDI:WG Production") +
  theme(
  panel.background = element_rect(fill = NA),
  panel.grid.major = element_line(colour = "lightgrey"),
  text = element_text(size=16)
)

The scatterplot above shows increasing errors at both extremes of the ability level. Perhaps due to floor and ceiling effects. Errors higher than 0.1 highly unfrequent though:

hist(scores$SE_F1, main = "Norwegian CDI:WG Production", sub = "Histogram of SE", xlab = "SE")

We can export the data for crosslinguistic plotting/analysing.

write_csv(scores, "Data/scores_Norwegian-WG-prod.csv")

SE and ability level vs. age

The graph below shows that higher error rates are at and close to age range limits (which is sort of obvious, given the relation between theta and age). But it also shows that some outliers are at every age (though in the middle they are not as high).

ggplot(data.frame(age = as.factor(scores$age), SE = scores$SE_F1), aes(age, SE)) +
  geom_boxplot() +
  xlab("Age (months)") +
  ylab("Standard error of ability estimations") +
  labs(title = "Norwegian CDI:WG Production") +
  theme(
  panel.background = element_rect(fill = NA),
  panel.grid.major = element_line(colour = "lightgrey"),
  text = element_text(size=16)
  )

So let’s see the relation between ability level and age (and first between raw scores and age). We add SE as colour.

ggplot(scores) +
  geom_point(aes(age, score))

ggplot(scores) +
  geom_point(aes(age, F1, col = SE_F1)) +
  scale_fill_gradient(low="green", high="red", aesthetics = "col") +
  labs(y = "ability level", col = "SE") +
  ylim(-4, 4)

Simulations

params <- as.data.frame(coef(mod, simplify = T)$items)[1:2]
mo <- generate.mirt_object(params, '2PL')
cl <- makeCluster(detectCores())

Whole pool for everyone

message(paste("Starting simulation @ ", Sys.time()))
results_all <- mirtCAT(mo = mo, method = "MAP", criteria = "MI", start_item = "MI",
                       local_pattern = responses, cl = cl, design = list(min_items = ncol(responses)))
# results_all1 <- mirtCAT(mo = mod, method = "MAP", criteria = "MI", start_item = "MI",
#                       local_pattern = responses_r, cl = cl, design = list(min_items = ncol(responses_r)))
save(results_all, file = "Data/norwegian_wg_prod_sim_all.Rdata")
message(paste("Finished @ ", Sys.time()))
beep()
load("Data/norwegian_wg_prod_sim_all.Rdata")
report_sim_results(results_all, select(scores, contains("F1")))
## [1] "Mean length: 390  Median length: 390  Correlation: 1  Mean SE: 0.192  Reliability: 0.963  Unused items: 0"

Based on the whole pool simulation we can examine decreasing average SE with each item (we plot it up to 100 items: no need for more).

SE_history <- laply(results_all, function(x) x$thetas_SE_history)
meanSE_item <- as.data.frame(colMeans(SE_history))
meanSE_item$item <- row.names(meanSE_item)
colnames(meanSE_item) <- c("mean_SE", "item")
meanSE_item$item <- as.numeric(meanSE_item$item)

ggline(meanSE_item, x = "item", y = "mean_SE", numeric.x.axis = TRUE) +
  xlab ("Test length") +
  ylab ("Mean SE") +
  labs(title = "Norwegian CDI:WG comp") +
  theme(
    panel.background = element_rect(fill = NA),
    panel.grid.major = element_line(colour = "lightgrey"),
    text = element_text(size=16)
  ) + 
  scale_y_continuous(breaks = c(0.1, 0.15, 0.2, 0.25, 0.5, 0.75, 1)) + 
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = seq(0, nrow(params), by=10), limits = c(1, 100))

We can export the data for crosslinguistic plotting/analysing.

write_csv(meanSE_item, "Data/meanSE_Norwegian-WG-prod.csv")

SE = 0.1 stop criterion

The plot above shows that we need 30-40 items to reach SE=.1 on average. Let’s try a simulation.

results_SE1 <- sim_se(0.1, file = "Data/norwegian_wg_prod_sim_se1.RData")
load("Data/norwegian_wg_prod_sim_se1.RData")
results_SE1 <- results
report_sim_results(results_SE1, select(scores, contains("F1")))
## [1] "Mean length: 248.9  Median length: 390  Correlation: 0.997  Mean SE: 0.209  Reliability: 0.956  Unused items: 0"
plot_length(results_SE1, "Norwegian CDI:WG Prod", 0.1)

SE = 0.15 stop criterion

 results_SE15 <- sim_se(0.15, file = "Data/norwegian_wg_prod_sim_se15.RData")
beep()
load("Data/norwegian_wg_prod_sim_se15.RData")
results_SE15 <- results
report_sim_results(results_SE15, select(scores, contains("F1")))
## [1] "Mean length: 189.9  Median length: 56  Correlation: 0.993  Mean SE: 0.231  Reliability: 0.947  Unused items: 0"
plot_length(results_SE15, "Norwegian CDI:WG Prod", 0.15)
